To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the majority of farmers produce agricultural output and multiple non-marketed ecosystem in a complementary relationship; changing the composition of the non-markated ecosystem services output would result in a different cost-minimizing production strategy for the majority of farms; and the marginal cost of generating non-marketed ecosystem service is farm-specific.

the marginal costs of producing non-marketed outputs are not constant and depend on the production structure of individual farms and that the marginal cost of producing non-market outputs are higher when the level of non-marketed outputs is increased.

(i) the marginal cost of generating non-marketed ecosystem service changes with the composition of the marketed output; (ii) the marginal cost is lower for complementary than competitive relationships; and (iii) the marginal cost depends on the minimum acceptable level of ecosystem service production.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new approach for the valuation of ecosystem services and the design of green payment schemes.
the marginal costs of producing non-marketed ecosystem service outputs.
the economic nature of ecosystem services production, and the implications of this for the design and evaluation of green payment schemes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the production of multiple ecosystem services is complementary with the production of agricultural output.
the production structure of farms in the UK is highly complex, which makes it impossible to generalize.
the marginal costs of producing ecosystem services depend on the type of ecosystem service and the production structure of each farm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a change in the composition of ecosystem services would have very different impacts on individual farms and that the marginal cost of producing a unit of ecosystem services is highly dependent on the level of the ecosystem service.

the cost of marginal changes in ecosystem services depends on the type of production relationship between marketed outputs and ecosystem services, the type of ecosystem service, and the minimum acceptable level of ecosystem services.
there is a need to develop a new framework for assessing the cost-effectiveness of green payment schemes that considers the interactions between marketed output and non-marketed outputs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the marginal cost of ecosystem services is farm specific and depends on the composition of the marketed outputs and non-market outputs.
the production of marketed output and ecosystem services are interdependent.
the marginal costs of generating non-marketed ecosystem service depend not only on the level of the non-market output but also on the level of agricultural output.
